Welcome to the course. We will work through each concept carefully, connect the
ideas step by step, and use practical examples to make technical topics easier
to understand. When we introduce a new method, focus first on the problem it
solves and why it is useful. For example, in machine learning, features are the
information we give the model, while the target is what we want it to predict.
Now consider a simple question: what changes when the data contains missing
values? We will think through the reason and then look at the code. In Python,
we can inspect the data, run one small step at a time, and explain what the
result means. The goal is to understand the logic, not simply memorize syntax.

slides.title: Start
slides.transcript: Welcome to Module 7, Subqueries in PostgreSQL. A subquery is a query used inside another query. The important part is not the parentheses. The important part is understanding what the inner query returns and what the outer query expects. We will build this gradually, starting with result shapes and then moving through scalar subqueries, membership, existence, ANY and ALL, correlated subqueries, and derived tables. Every SQL example can run directly in the browser. You can also copy the query into pgAdmin for more practice. Keep a real project in mind as we work through this section—for example, a hospital identifying patients above a benchmark or with no follow-up. The technical feature matters because it changes what questions we can answer reliably and how easily another analyst can understand our work. As you listen, try to connect each SQL or data concept to a decision you might need to defend later: what the data means, what one row represents, what can be missing, and what assumptions the transformation introduces.

slides.title: Why subqueries matter
slides.transcript: Subqueries become useful when one part of the question depends on the result of another query. Sometimes the inner query produces one benchmark such as average age. Sometimes it produces a set of patient IDs. Sometimes we only need to know whether a matching related row exists. And sometimes the inner query depends on the current outer row. These are different contracts, and recognizing the contract is more useful than memorizing syntax. Connect this idea to an e-commerce team finding customers who purchased a target product. Ask what could go wrong if the concept were misunderstood: could rows be duplicated, important records disappear, categories be interpreted incorrectly, or a report become difficult to reproduce? A strong analyst can explain both the SQL operation and the assumption behind it. After the example, summarize the idea in one plain-language sentence before moving on.

slides.title: Prerequisite review
slides.transcript: Module 7 builds on earlier SQL ideas. You should already recognize basic SELECT queries, aggregate functions, simple joins, and NULL. Subqueries combine those familiar pieces in a new structure. If you can read a simple query on its own, the main new skill is understanding how the result of one query is used by another. Connect this idea to a compliance workflow checking whether related evidence exists. Ask what could go wrong if the concept were misunderstood: could rows be duplicated, important records disappear, categories be interpreted incorrectly, or a report become difficult to reproduce? A strong analyst can explain both the SQL operation and the assumption behind it. After the example, summarize the idea in one plain-language sentence before moving on.

slides.title: Module roadmap
slides.transcript: We will start with the result shape of the inner query. Then we will learn scalar subqueries, followed by set-oriented patterns such as IN, EXISTS, ANY, and ALL. After that, we will study correlated subqueries, where the inner query depends on the current outer row. Finally, we will compare placements and rewrites. This order makes subqueries easier to understand because every new pattern answers a specific kind of question. Keep a real project in mind as we work through this section—for example, a hospital identifying patients above a benchmark or with no follow-up. The technical feature matters because it changes what questions we can answer reliably and how easily another analyst can understand our work. As you listen, try to connect each SQL or data concept to a decision you might need to defend later: what the data means, what one row represents, what can be missing, and what assumptions the transformation introduces.

slides.title: Running database
slides.transcript: The module uses a small healthcare-style teaching database. Patients is the main entity. Admissions, lab results, and prescriptions connect back to patients. Admissions also connect to departments. The review queue contains one patient ID and one deliberate NULL. That NULL is important because we will use it to demonstrate the NOT IN trap. The database loads automatically in the browser. Connect this idea to an e-commerce team finding customers who purchased a target product. slides.title: Relationship map
slides.transcript: Most examples in this module depend on the same relationship. A patient can have many admissions, many lab results, and many prescriptions. When you see a correlated condition such as a dot patient ID equals p dot patient ID, it is connecting a child row to the current patient row. Keeping the relationship map simple lets us focus on the subquery behavior rather than on a complicated schema. Connect this idea to a compliance workflow checking whether related evidence exists. slides.transcript: Before writing nested queries, inspect the underlying rows. Run this simple SELECT and look at the patient IDs and ages. Later, when the subquery returns a set of IDs or an average age, you will be able to connect the result back to real rows in the teaching dataset. This is also a good real-world habit. slides.title: The main mental model
slides.transcript: The best mental model is to treat the inner query as a result producer. The inner query produces something. The outer query then uses that result. The result might be one value, a set of values, or rows that behave like an intermediate table. Before writing the SQL, ask what shape the outer query needs. That question prevents many common subquery errors. Connect this idea to an e-commerce team finding customers who purchased a target product. Ask what could go wrong if the concept were misunderstood: could rows be duplicated, important records disappear, categories be interpreted incorrectly, or a report become difficult to reproduce? A strong analyst can explain both the SQL operation and the assumption behind it. After the example, summarize the idea in one plain-language sentence before moving on.

slides.title: Three common result shapes
slides.transcript: Three ideas appear repeatedly. A scalar subquery behaves like one value. A set subquery returns zero or more values, usually from one column. A correlated subquery refers to the current outer row, so its result can change as the outer row changes. When you identify the shape and dependency, the SQL operator becomes easier to choose. A subquery has a contract: it returns a shape. A scalar subquery must return at most one value where it is used. Before writing syntax, predict whether the inner query returns one value, one column with many rows, or a table. Shape mistakes are easier to prevent than to debug after the query becomes large.

slides.title: Shape before syntax
slides.transcript: This table turns business questions into subquery contracts. One benchmark suggests a scalar. Membership in a returned list suggests IN. Existence of any matching row suggests EXISTS. At least one comparison suggests ANY, while every comparison suggests ALL. A per-row calculation often uses a correlated scalar. This translation from question to contract is the main skill of the module. A subquery has a contract: it returns a shape. A scalar subquery must return at most one value where it is used. Before writing syntax, predict whether the inner query returns one value, one column with many rows, or a table. Shape mistakes are easier to prevent than to debug after the query becomes large.

slides.title: Scalar subquery contract
slides.transcript: A scalar subquery has a strict result contract. It returns one column and at most one row. One row gives the scalar value. Zero rows become NULL. More than one row is an error because the surrounding expression expected one value. Understanding this contract is more important than remembering where the parentheses go. When reading the example, do not read punctuation one character at a time. Start with the purpose of the query, then identify the input rows, the operation being applied, and the shape of the expected output. In a real setting such as an e-commerce team finding customers who purchased a target product, this habit makes code reviews much easier because you can explain what the query is supposed to guarantee before discussing syntax. After running it, inspect a few records manually and check that the result matches that explanation.

slides.title: Scalar in WHERE
slides.transcript: The inner query calculates average age across all patients. That produces one number. The outer WHERE clause compares each patient age with that one benchmark. Read the condition as a sentence: keep the patient when age is greater than the average age returned by the inner query. Run the query and compare the returned ages with the full patient list. A subquery has a contract: it returns a shape. A scalar subquery must return at most one value where it is used. Before writing syntax, predict whether the inner query returns one value, one column with many rows, or a table. Shape mistakes are easier to prevent than to debug after the query becomes large.

slides.title: Read a scalar query step by step
slides.transcript: When a scalar query feels confusing, isolate the inner query mentally. Ask what it returns. Here it returns one average age. Now imagine replacing the parenthesized SELECT with that number. The outer query becomes an ordinary age comparison. This simple mental substitution works well for many scalar subqueries. When reading the example, do not read punctuation one character at a time. Start with the purpose of the query, then identify the input rows, the operation being applied, and the shape of the expected output. In a real setting such as a hospital identifying patients above a benchmark or with no follow-up, this habit makes code reviews much easier because you can explain what the query is supposed to guarantee before discussing syntax. After running it, inspect a few records manually and check that the result matches that explanation.

slides.title: Scalar in SELECT
slides.transcript: A scalar subquery can also appear in the SELECT list. Here, the inner query calculates one overall average age. Because it is not correlated, the same value appears beside every patient row. This is useful when you want to show a row value and a benchmark together. Run the query and notice that the average does not change from patient to patient. A subquery has a contract: it returns a shape. A scalar subquery must return at most one value where it is used. Before writing syntax, predict whether the inner query returns one value, one column with many rows, or a table. Shape mistakes are easier to prevent than to debug after the query becomes large.

slides.title: Scalar with zero rows
slides.transcript: A scalar subquery may return zero rows. When that happens, PostgreSQL turns the missing scalar into NULL. The requested test ID in this example does not exist. So the inner query returns no row, and the scalar result becomes NULL. Remember this when the scalar participates in a comparison, because comparisons involving NULL follow three-valued logic. A subquery has a contract: it returns a shape. A scalar subquery must return at most one value where it is used. Before writing syntax, predict whether the inner query returns one value, one column with many rows, or a table. Shape mistakes are easier to prevent than to debug after the query becomes large.

slides.title: Scalar with too many rows
slides.transcript: Now we deliberately violate the scalar contract. The inner query returns many patient IDs from admissions. The outer expression expects one value. PostgreSQL cannot choose one row for you, so it raises an error. Do not automatically add LIMIT one just to remove the error. Only do that if choosing an arbitrary single row actually matches the business meaning. A subquery has a contract: it returns a shape. A scalar subquery must return at most one value where it is used. Before writing syntax, predict whether the inner query returns one value, one column with many rows, or a table. Shape mistakes are easier to prevent than to debug after the query becomes large.

slides.title: Scalar checklist
slides.transcript: Before using a scalar subquery, ask three questions. Does it return one column? Can it ever return more than one row? And what should happen if it returns no row? This small checklist catches most scalar-subquery problems before you run the query. A subquery has a contract: it returns a shape. A scalar subquery must return at most one value where it is used. Before writing syntax, predict whether the inner query returns one value, one column with many rows, or a table. Shape mistakes are easier to prevent than to debug after the query becomes large.

slides.title: IN means membership
slides.transcript: IN is a membership operator. The inner query should return a one-column set. The outer value is compared with the values in that set. If it matches one of them, the membership test succeeds. Think of IN as asking, is this value in that returned list? IN answers a membership question: is this value present in the set returned by the subquery? Be especially careful with NOT IN when NULL can appear in that set, because three-valued logic can turn expected TRUE results into UNKNOWN. For anti-matching, NOT EXISTS is often easier to reason about.

slides.title: IN example
slides.transcript: The inner query returns patient IDs from Cardiology admissions. The outer query keeps patients whose patient ID appears in that set. This is a natural use of IN because the business question is membership. Run the query and connect each returned patient with the Cardiology admissions table. When reading the example, do not read punctuation one character at a time. Start with the purpose of the query, then identify the input rows, the operation being applied, and the shape of the expected output. In a real setting such as a hospital identifying patients above a benchmark or with no follow-up, this habit makes code reviews much easier because you can explain what the query is supposed to guarantee before discussing syntax. After running it, inspect a few records manually and check that the result matches that explanation.

slides.title: IN is not a JOIN
slides.transcript: IN and JOIN may appear to answer similar questions, but they have different semantics. IN asks whether an outer value belongs to a set. A join returns matching row combinations. If one patient has multiple admissions, the join can repeat that patient. The IN query keeps the patient-level outer grain. Run both queries and compare the outputs carefully. Connect this idea to an e-commerce team finding customers who purchased a target product. Ask what could go wrong if the concept were misunderstood: could rows be duplicated, important records disappear, categories be interpreted incorrectly, or a report become difficult to reproduce? A strong analyst can explain both the SQL operation and the assumption behind it. After the example, summarize the idea in one plain-language sentence before moving on.

slides.title: NOT IN looks simple
slides.transcript: NOT IN looks like a simple anti-membership test. But if the inner set contains NULL, PostgreSQL cannot prove that an outer value differs from the unknown value. The condition can become UNKNOWN rather than TRUE. Because WHERE keeps only TRUE, rows you expected may disappear. This is one of the most important edge cases in this module. IN answers a membership question: is this value present in the set returned by the subquery? Be especially careful with NOT IN when NULL can appear in that set, because three-valued logic can turn expected TRUE results into UNKNOWN. For anti-matching, NOT EXISTS is often easier to reason about.

slides.title: Three-valued logic
slides.transcript: SQL uses three-valued logic. A condition can be TRUE, FALSE, or UNKNOWN. Comparing a normal value with NULL gives UNKNOWN, not FALSE. And NOT UNKNOWN remains UNKNOWN. Because WHERE returns only rows whose condition is TRUE, UNKNOWN behaves like a filtered-out row. This explains the NOT IN behavior. Connect this idea to a hospital identifying patients above a benchmark or with no follow-up. Ask what could go wrong if the concept were misunderstood: could rows be duplicated, important records disappear, categories be interpreted incorrectly, or a report become difficult to reproduce? A strong analyst can explain both the SQL operation and the assumption behind it. After the example, summarize the idea in one plain-language sentence before moving on.

slides.title: NOT IN + NULL trap
slides.transcript: The review queue contains patient 1003 and a NULL. For another patient such as 1001, PostgreSQL knows 1001 is not equal to 1003. But it cannot know whether 1001 is different from the NULL value. That unknown comparison prevents the full NOT IN condition from becoming TRUE. Run the query and observe the result. IN answers a membership question: is this value present in the set returned by the subquery? Be especially careful with NOT IN when NULL can appear in that set, because three-valued logic can turn expected TRUE results into UNKNOWN. For anti-matching, NOT EXISTS is often easier to reason about.

slides.title: Safer anti-match
slides.transcript: NOT EXISTS expresses the anti-match directly. For each patient, the inner query searches for a review-queue row with the same patient ID. If no matching row exists, the patient is kept. The unrelated NULL row does not create the same problem because it does not match the current patient ID. This is why NOT EXISTS is often the clearer starting point for anti-join questions. EXISTS asks whether at least one related row satisfies the condition. The selected columns inside EXISTS usually do not matter; the existence of a row does. This maps naturally to questions such as patients with any follow-up, customers with any purchase, or orders with no shipment record.

slides.title: EXISTS means existence
slides.transcript: EXISTS asks only whether the inner query returns at least one row. The actual selected value inside the subquery usually does not matter. That is why SELECT one is common. The business meaning is simply: does any related row satisfy this condition? This makes EXISTS especially natural for relationship checks. EXISTS asks whether at least one related row satisfies the condition. The selected columns inside EXISTS usually do not matter; the existence of a row does. This maps naturally to questions such as patients with any follow-up, customers with any purchase, or orders with no shipment record.

slides.title: EXISTS example
slides.transcript: For each patient, the inner query searches lab results for the same patient ID. It looks for any result outside the normal range. We do not need a count. We only need at least one abnormal row. That makes EXISTS a direct match for the question. Run the query and identify the patients that satisfy the condition. When reading the example, do not read punctuation one character at a time. Start with the purpose of the query, then identify the input rows, the operation being applied, and the shape of the expected output. In a real setting such as an e-commerce team finding customers who purchased a target product, this habit makes code reviews much easier because you can explain what the query is supposed to guarantee before discussing syntax. After running it, inspect a few records manually and check that the result matches that explanation.

slides.title: NOT EXISTS example
slides.transcript: NOT EXISTS asks whether no matching row can be found. For each patient, the inner query searches prescriptions. If there is no prescription with that patient ID, the patient is returned. This pattern appears everywhere: customers with no orders, students with no submissions, devices with no alerts, and patients with no prescription record. When reading the example, do not read punctuation one character at a time. Start with the purpose of the query, then identify the input rows, the operation being applied, and the shape of the expected output. In a real setting such as a compliance workflow checking whether related evidence exists, this habit makes code reviews much easier because you can explain what the query is supposed to guarantee before discussing syntax. After running it, inspect a few records manually and check that the result matches that explanation.

slides.title: IN vs EXISTS
slides.transcript: IN and EXISTS can sometimes be rewritten into equivalent forms. But when writing the first version, choose the operator that expresses the business question clearly. Membership suggests IN. Existence suggests EXISTS. Absence of a related match suggests NOT EXISTS. Clear semantics make the query easier to explain, review, and debug. EXISTS asks whether at least one related row satisfies the condition. The selected columns inside EXISTS usually do not matter; the existence of a row does. This maps naturally to questions such as patients with any follow-up, customers with any purchase, or orders with no shipment record.

slides.title: ANY, SOME, and ALL
slides.transcript: ANY and ALL compare one outer value with an entire set. ANY means at least one comparison must succeed. ALL means every comparison must succeed. PostgreSQL also supports SOME as a synonym for ANY. The difference sounds small, but it can produce very different result sets. ANY and ALL compare one value with a set. ANY needs the comparison to succeed against at least one returned value; ALL requires it to succeed against every returned value. Empty sets and NULLs can affect the result, so test those cases explicitly when the set is data-driven.

slides.title: ANY example
slides.transcript: Greater than ANY means the outer age must be greater than at least one age returned by the inner query. For a nonempty set without NULL complications, a helpful intuition is to compare with the minimum. If your age is greater than the smallest returned age, at least one comparison succeeds. Run the query and compare the result with that intuition. When reading the example, do not read punctuation one character at a time. Start with the purpose of the query, then identify the input rows, the operation being applied, and the shape of the expected output. In a real setting such as a compliance workflow checking whether related evidence exists, this habit makes code reviews much easier because you can explain what the query is supposed to guarantee before discussing syntax. After running it, inspect a few records manually and check that the result matches that explanation.

slides.title: ALL example
slides.transcript: Greater than ALL is stricter. The outer age must be greater than every age returned by the inner query. A useful intuition is to compare with the maximum. To be greater than all returned ages, the outer value must exceed the largest one. Run the query and compare the row count with the ANY example. Start with the purpose of the query, then identify the input rows, the operation being applied, and the shape of the expected output. In a real setting such as a hospital identifying patients above a benchmark or with no follow-up, this habit makes code reviews much easier because you can explain what the query is supposed to guarantee before discussing syntax. After running it, inspect a few records manually and check that the result matches that explanation.

slides.title: ANY vs ALL
slides.transcript: ANY and ALL can be summarized with a simple contrast. ANY needs at least one successful comparison. ALL needs every comparison to succeed. Equality with ANY behaves much like IN. These are useful intuitions, but always remember that NULL values and empty sets can affect the formal SQL logic. ANY and ALL compare one value with a set. ANY needs the comparison to succeed against at least one returned value; ALL requires it to succeed against every returned value. Empty sets and NULLs can affect the result, so test those cases explicitly when the set is data-driven.

slides.title: Empty set behavior
slides.transcript: Empty sets create an important edge case. ANY needs at least one successful comparison. If the set is empty, no comparison can succeed, so ANY is FALSE. ALL asks whether every comparison succeeds. With no values, there is no failing comparison, so ALL is TRUE. This can feel surprising, but it follows the logic of existential and universal conditions. A strong analyst can explain both the SQL operation and the assumption behind it. After the example, summarize the idea in one plain-language sentence before moving on.

slides.title: Correlated subqueries
slides.transcript: A correlated subquery uses a value from the current outer row. For example, the outer query may define patients as p. Inside the subquery, a condition may compare a child patient ID with p patient ID. When the outer patient changes, the inner query's matching value changes too. This is why correlated subqueries are useful for per-row calculations. A correlated subquery refers to the current row of the outer query. Conceptually, the inner query is evaluated in relation to each outer row. That makes some business rules easy to express, but it can be expensive at scale. Compare a correlated formulation with a pre-aggregated join when performance matters.

slides.title: How to spot correlation
slides.transcript: To identify correlation, look for an alias that was defined outside the subquery but used inside it. If the inner query needs p patient ID from the outer patient row, it is correlated. A quick diagnostic is to ask whether the inner query can run meaningfully by itself unchanged. If it needs an outer value, the answer is no. A correlated subquery refers to the current row of the outer query. Conceptually, the inner query is evaluated in relation to each outer row. That makes some business rules easy to express, but it can be expensive at scale. Compare a correlated formulation with a pre-aggregated join when performance matters.

slides.title: Correlated benchmark
slides.transcript: This query uses correlation to calculate a test-specific benchmark. For a Glucose row, the inner query calculates the average Glucose result. For a Cholesterol row, it calculates the average Cholesterol result. The outer test name changes the inner query. This is a powerful pattern when one global benchmark would not be meaningful. A correlated subquery refers to the current row of the outer query. Conceptually, the inner query is evaluated in relation to each outer row. That makes some business rules easy to express, but it can be expensive at scale. Compare a correlated formulation with a pre-aggregated join when performance matters.

slides.title: Trace one correlated row
slides.transcript: A correlated query becomes easier if you trace one outer row at a time. Imagine the current row is a Glucose test. The inner query uses the outer test name to average only Glucose values. Then the current result is compared with that benchmark. When the outer row changes to another test, the inner benchmark changes as well. A correlated subquery refers to the current row of the outer query. Conceptually, the inner query is evaluated in relation to each outer row. That makes some business rules easy to express, but it can be expensive at scale. Compare a correlated formulation with a pre-aggregated join when performance matters.

slides.title: Correlated count in SELECT
slides.transcript: A correlated scalar subquery can appear in SELECT. For each patient, the inner query counts admissions for that patient ID. COUNT returns one scalar value, so the scalar contract is satisfied. The result keeps one row per patient while adding an admission count. This form is direct and easy to read for a simple per-row metric. IN answers a membership question: is this value present in the set returned by the subquery? Be especially careful with NOT IN when NULL can appear in that set, because three-valued logic can turn expected TRUE results into UNKNOWN. For anti-matching, NOT EXISTS is often easier to reason about.

slides.title: Latest related row
slides.transcript: This pattern finds the latest admission for each patient. For the current patient, the inner query finds the maximum admission date. The outer admission row is kept when its date equals that patient-specific maximum. This pattern is useful for latest order, latest event, newest status, or most recent activity. If two rows share the same maximum date, both can be returned. Connect this idea to a compliance workflow checking whether related evidence exists. A strong analyst can explain both the SQL operation and the assumption behind it. After the example, summarize the idea in one plain-language sentence before moving on.

slides.title: Subquery placement
slides.transcript: Subqueries can appear in different clauses because each clause expects a different role. A subquery in WHERE contributes to filtering. A scalar subquery in SELECT becomes an output value. A subquery in FROM becomes an intermediate table. Choose the placement based on what you need the inner result to do. When reading the example, do not read punctuation one character at a time. Start with the purpose of the query, then identify the input rows, the operation being applied, and the shape of the expected output. In a real setting such as a hospital identifying patients above a benchmark or with no follow-up, this habit makes code reviews much easier because you can explain what the query is supposed to guarantee before discussing syntax. After running it, inspect a few records manually and check that the result matches that explanation.

slides.title: Subquery in WHERE
slides.transcript: WHERE is the most familiar location for subqueries. The inner result can become a benchmark, a membership set, an existence condition, or a set comparison. The final job is always Boolean: should the current outer row remain? That is why many subquery patterns appear naturally in WHERE. When reading the example, do not read punctuation one character at a time. Start with the purpose of the query, then identify the input rows, the operation being applied, and the shape of the expected output. In a real setting such as an e-commerce team finding customers who purchased a target product, this habit makes code reviews much easier because you can explain what the query is supposed to guarantee before discussing syntax. After running it, inspect a few records manually and check that the result matches that explanation.

slides.title: Subquery in SELECT
slides.transcript: A subquery in SELECT must behave like a scalar for each output row. If it is uncorrelated, the same value may repeat. If it is correlated, the value can change from row to row. This placement is useful when you want to enrich each row with one related summary value. When reading the example, do not read punctuation one character at a time. Start with the purpose of the query, then identify the input rows, the operation being applied, and the shape of the expected output. In a real setting such as a compliance workflow checking whether related evidence exists, this habit makes code reviews much easier because you can explain what the query is supposed to guarantee before discussing syntax. After running it, inspect a few records manually and check that the result matches that explanation.

slides.title: Derived tables
slides.transcript: A subquery in FROM is called a derived table. The inner query produces rows and columns. The outer query treats those rows like an intermediate table for that statement. This is especially useful when you want to aggregate first and then join. Always ask what one row in the derived table represents. SQL can express the same logic in several forms. A good rewrite keeps the same grain and business meaning while changing how work is organized. Use EXPLAIN to inspect the plan rather than assuming one style is always faster. Performance reasoning should follow correctness, not replace it.

slides.title: Derived table example
slides.transcript: The inner query groups admissions by patient ID. That creates one admission-count row per patient ID. The outer query left joins those counts to the patient table. COALESCE converts missing counts to zero for patients with no admissions. This pattern makes the intermediate grain very clear. When reading the example, do not read punctuation one character at a time. Start with the purpose of the query, then identify the input rows, the operation being applied, and the shape of the expected output. In a real setting such as an e-commerce team finding customers who purchased a target product, this habit makes code reviews much easier because you can explain what the query is supposed to guarantee before discussing syntax. After running it, inspect a few records manually and check that the result matches that explanation.

slides.title: Correlated vs pre-aggregated
slides.transcript: A correlated scalar and a pre-aggregated join can sometimes produce the same result. The correlated form may be simpler to read. The derived-table form may be convenient when several aggregated features are needed. Do not assume one form is always faster. PostgreSQL can transform queries during optimization. Use correct semantics first, then inspect the plan on representative data. A correlated subquery refers to the current row of the outer query. Conceptually, the inner query is evaluated in relation to each outer row. That makes some business rules easy to express, but it can be expensive at scale. Compare a correlated formulation with a pre-aggregated join when performance matters.

slides.title: Rewrite example
slides.transcript: This query rewrites the admission-count problem. The inner query groups admissions once by patient ID. The outer query joins those counts to patients. Run it and compare the result with the correlated scalar version. The business meaning and patient-level grain should remain the same. When rewriting, always verify that the result did not change. When reading the example, do not read punctuation one character at a time. Start with the purpose of the query, then identify the input rows, the operation being applied, and the shape of the expected output. In a real setting such as a hospital identifying patients above a benchmark or with no follow-up, this habit makes code reviews much easier because you can explain what the query is supposed to guarantee before discussing syntax. After running it, inspect a few records manually and check that the result matches that explanation.

slides.title: EXPLAIN
slides.transcript: EXPLAIN shows PostgreSQL's planned execution strategy. This is useful for learning how the database intends to access and combine rows. In this tiny browser dataset, use the plan only to learn structure. Real performance tuning requires representative data volume, indexes, statistics, and workload. Do not make production performance claims from a small teaching example. SQL can express the same logic in several forms. A good rewrite keeps the same grain and business meaning while changing how work is organized. Use EXPLAIN to inspect the plan rather than assuming one style is always faster. Performance reasoning should follow correctness, not replace it.

slides.title: Performance principles
slides.transcript: Performance should come after correctness. A faster query that changes row grain or NULL behavior is not an improvement. Write the clearest correct query first. Then inspect the execution plan and consider rewrites or indexes. Whenever you rewrite a subquery, compare the result sets carefully. SQL can express the same logic in several forms. A good rewrite keeps the same grain and business meaning while changing how work is organized. Use EXPLAIN to inspect the plan rather than assuming one style is always faster. Performance reasoning should follow correctness, not replace it.

slides.title: Pattern decision guide

slides.title: Applied challenge
slides.transcript: This challenge asks for patients whose admission count is above the average admission count among patients who have at least one admission. Break the task into stages. First create patient-level admission counts. Then calculate the average of those counts. Finally compare each patient's count with that average. Use the starter and test the query incrementally rather than writing everything at once. ANY and ALL compare one value with a set. ANY needs the comparison to succeed against at least one returned value; ALL requires it to succeed against every returned value. slides.title: Module 7 takeaways
slides.transcript: These are the key contracts. Scalar means one value. IN means membership. EXISTS means existence. ANY and ALL compare one value with a set. Correlation means the inner query depends on the current outer row. A derived table means the inner query produces rows for the outer query to use. If you understand the meaning, you can rebuild the syntax when needed. Connect this idea to a compliance workflow checking whether related evidence exists. slides.title: Final decision guide
slides.transcript: Use this final guide when you are unsure. Ask what the outer query needs from the inner query. One value suggests a scalar. Membership suggests IN. A related-row question suggests EXISTS or NOT EXISTS. A comparison against a set suggests ANY or ALL. Intermediate rows suggest a derived table. Then ask whether the inner query depends on the current outer row. If yes, it is correlated. Connect this idea to a hospital identifying patients above a benchmark or with no follow-up.
